title: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities

hero.subtitle: The hierarchical naming system that maps human-readable names to IP addresses

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed, hierarchical naming system that translates human-readable domain names (like www.example.com) into IP addresses (like 192.0.2.1) and other resource records.

RFC 1034 defines the concepts behind DNS, while its companion RFC 1035 details the implementation. Together, they form the foundation of the Internet's naming infrastructure.

Before DNS, host name-to-address mappings were maintained in a single HOSTS.TXT file distributed to every machine. As the Internet grew, this approach became completely unmanageable.
sections.eli5: Long ago everyone shared one big list of computer names and had to ask one office to change it. As more computers joined, that office could not keep up. DNS gives each group its own small list, plus a way to find the right list.

sections.title: Domain Name Space
sections.content:
The domain name space is a tree structure where each node has a label up to 63 characters long. A domain name is the sequence of labels from a node to the root, separated by dots.

Root Domain
The root of the tree is represented by an empty label (or a trailing dot). The root zone is managed by IANA and served by 13 root server clusters (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net).
Top-Level Domains (TLDs)
Direct children of the root include generic TLDs (.com, .org, .net) and country-code TLDs (.uk, .de, .jp). Each TLD is managed by a designated registry.
Zones and Delegation
The name space is divided into zones, each managed by a particular authority. A zone can delegate subdomains to other name servers, creating a distributed administration model.

A fully-qualified domain name (FQDN) includes the trailing dot representing the root: www.example.com. — though the trailing dot is usually omitted in everyday use.
sections.eli5: Names are like a family tree upside down. At the top is one ancestor with no name, then big branches like com and org, then smaller branches. To write a name you list the branches from you up to the top, with dots in between.

sections.title: Name Servers
sections.content:
Name servers store DNS data and respond to queries. They are organized hierarchically, matching the structure of the domain name space.

Server Type
Role
Example
Root Server
Knows TLD authoritative servers
a.root-servers.net
TLD Server
Knows domain authoritative servers
a.gtld-servers.net
Authoritative
Holds actual DNS records for a zone
ns1.example.com
Recursive Resolver
Resolves queries on behalf of clients
8.8.8.8 (Google)

Each zone must have at least two authoritative name servers for redundancy. The primary server holds the master copy of zone data; secondary servers receive copies via zone transfers.
sections.eli5: Name servers are the helpers that keep the lists. Some know only who to ask next, and some hold the real answers for one family branch. Every branch needs more than one helper so it still works if one is asleep.

sections.title: Resolvers
sections.content:
Resolvers are the client side of DNS, responsible for translating application queries into the protocol messages needed to find answers.

Stub Resolver
A minimal resolver built into the operating system. It sends recursive queries to a configured DNS server and relies on that server to do the full resolution.
Recursive Resolver
A full-service resolver that follows the chain of delegations from root to authoritative server. It caches results to speed up future queries.
Iterative vs. Recursive
In iterative resolution, a server returns a referral to the next server to ask. In recursive resolution, the server takes full responsibility for finding the answer on behalf of the client.
sections.eli5: A resolver is the person who goes asking on your behalf. Your computer asks a nearby helper, and that helper walks from the top of the tree, asking each level where to go next, until someone gives the answer.

sections.title: Caching
sections.content:
Caching is fundamental to DNS performance. Without caching, every DNS lookup would require traversing the hierarchy from root servers.

TTL (Time to Live)Each record has a TTL specifying how long it may be cached (in seconds)
Positive CachingSuccessful lookups are cached for the duration of the TTL
Negative CachingNXDOMAIN (name not found) results are also cached (RFC 2308)
Cache PoisoningAn attack where forged responses inject false entries into the cache

Setting TTL values involves a trade-off: low TTLs allow faster propagation of changes but increase query load on authoritative servers. High TTLs reduce load but make changes slow to propagate.
sections.eli5: Once the helper finds an answer it writes it on a sticky note and reuses it for a while, so it does not have to ask again. Each answer says how long the note is good for. Short notes mean fresh answers, long notes mean fewer questions.

references.text: Mockapetris, P., "Domain Names - Implementation and Specification", RFC 1035, November 1987.
Elz, R. and R. Bush, "Clarifications to the DNS Specification", RFC 2181, July 1997.

subtitle: The hierarchical naming system that maps human-readable names to IP addresses
summary: RFC 1034 describes the concepts behind the Domain Name System: a tree of names, split into zones that are served by name servers, and looked up on behalf of programs by resolvers. It replaced the single shared HOSTS.TXT file with a distributed database in which each organization manages its own part. The wire format and record types are in the companion RFC 1035.

eli5.summary: Instead of one giant phone book for the whole world, every neighborhood keeps its own page, and a helper knows which neighborhood to ask about any name.

tldr.problem: One central HOSTS.TXT file could not keep up with the growing Internet, because every change had to go through a single site and be copied to every host.
tldr.mechanism: Names form a tree. Each part of the tree is a zone run by its own authority and served by name servers. Resolvers follow referrals down from the root and cache what they learn for a time limit set by the record.
tldr.outcome: Naming became distributed and scalable, and this design is still how Internet names are looked up, with RFC 1035 supplying the wire format.

today: The tree of names, zones, delegation and caching described here is still how DNS works. Much has been added on top, including DNSSEC for signed answers and encrypted transports such as DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS, and later RFCs clarify and extend this one. RFC 1034 remains the standard starting point for understanding the model.
